title: Enigma’s fatal flaw: no letter could ever be encrypted as itself
body: Every key press stepped Enigma's rotors, so the scrambling changed with each letter. The current ran through the rotors to a **reflector**, which sent it back by a different route; that made the cipher reciprocal, so the same setting that turned A into B also turned B back into A. But it also meant a letter could never come out as itself. Allied codebreakers, building on Polish breakthroughs, used that to test guessed words called cribs: any position where a guessed letter lined up with the same letter in the ciphertext could be ruled out at once.

slides.alt: Animation of a simplified Enigma in a walnut box: pressing A five times lights B, D, Z, G and O as the right rotor steps. A diagram traces the current through three rotors to the reflector and back to a different letter, then the crib WETTER slides along a ciphertext, ruling out positions.

slides.question: Under the crib WETTER, one stretch of ciphertext reads XEPQAB. Could the crib sit there?
options: No: an E lines up with an E
Only if the rotors were reset
slides.explanation: The second letters match: E above E. Enigma never turned a letter into itself, so the crib can't sit there, plugboard or not.

slides.heading: Match the Enigma part to its job
slides.explanation: Operators normally plugged ten cables, swapping ten pairs; the reflector’s U-turn is what stops any letter encrypting as itself.

slides.heading: A simplified machine
slides.text: The animation leaves out the plugboard, which could swap up to 13 pairs of letters (10 were normal), and the rotors' ring settings. Neither fixes the flaw: the plugboard swaps the letter on the way in and back on the way out, so the reflector's rule still holds.
